highlights.text: a single regular root whose core sense is the tasting of a thing
طَعَام (ṭaʿām) is "that which is eaten," food.
Feeding (iṭʿām) covers anything ingested, even water.
a man well-off as to food, illustrated by al-Ḥuṭayʾa's line addressing "the well-fed, well-clothed one."
The ḥadīth "when the imam seeks 'food' from you, feed him" means: when he falters in recitation and seeks a prompt, supply the words for him.
a single sound root whose core sense is distinguishing and separating between two things
a piece split off from something when it splits apart
a genuine root whose senses cannot all be traced to one underlying idea, though they are of a related family
غُروب الشمس (sunset), as the sun's going far from the earth's face
الغُراب (well known)
الغِرْبِيب, deep black, seemingly from the crow's colour
رِجل الغُراب ("crow's foot"), a type of tight knot (verse by al-Kumayt)
*al-laẓā* means fire; some say specifically pure, smokeless flame.
Verbs *laẓiyat*, *iltaẓat*, *talaẓẓat* all mean "it (the fire) blazed."
A verse of al-Afwah is cited using it this way ("...as though the men were upon glowing coals and al-laẓā")
A hadith about Khayfān visiting ʿUthmān describes a tough clan as men "on whose spears death *tatalaẓẓā*" (blazes)
a sound root whose core meaning is al-laban, "milk" (the drink)
A short unattributed verse illustrates the pair: someone falsely claimed to be labin in summer and tamir with dates.
ملا (m-l-w/y) — extension in time and space, and dictation
ملأ (m-l-ʾ, with hamza) — fullness
a council/company united on one opinion, who "fill the eyes" with splendour and the souls with awe
al-milʾ = the capacity of a full vessel
a poet annexes malwā to "day and night" ("Day and night, whose malwā is unceasing…")
one sound root whose core sense is measuring-out / apportioning something (taqdīr) and the carrying-through of a decree (qaḍāʾ) upon it
مَنِيّ (semen) — the human fluid, so called because a person's formation is measured out from it
تَمَنِّي (wishing, longing): a hope a person measures out for himself
Shāhid from Ibn al-Ṭathriyya (the drinking-companion urging him to "rival the people in generosity")
as "when he recited, Satan cast into his recitation," glossing tamannā as "recited."
highlights.note: the author's own exegesis of Q 22:52

highlights.text: derives everything under this root (n-sh-ṭ) from one core meaning: **vibration and motion** (اهتزاز وحركة)
peeling draws the thing out from its own skin
Ibn Fāris cites a line of the poet Dhū al-Rumma describing such a bull — dappled-legged, dark-cheeked, a leader of its kind, a roaming young bull (نَاشِطٌ شَبَبُ) — as illustration.
The organising idea running through the entry is raised, standing up above a level.
نَشَزَ في مَجْلِسِه — to lift oneself up slightly in one's seat
أَنْشَزَ الشيءَ — to lift a thing from its place
نَشَزَت المرأةُ بِزَوجِها (she is ناشِز) — she rose up against him and came to detest him
Al-Aʿshā: "if you test my utmost mettle you will find in me a stout one, already grey, no weakling twin."
al-nabaz (fatḥa) = "a nickname/epithet"
tanābazū bi-l-alqāb = "they nicknamed one another." al-tanābuz = calling one another out by nicknames
this addressed Muslims calling converts "O Jew!" or "O Christian!" after their conversion
highlights.note: exegete Thaʿlab, who calls it weak

highlights.text: the verse means a Muslim must not taunt a former Jew or Christian, now Muslim, with a nickname recalling his former religion
Being unmindful of / neglecting a thing
Leaving / abandoning a thing
نَسِيتُ الشَّيْءَ ("I forgot it," when you fail to remember it)
النِّسْي — the worthless goods travellers drop and leave at a campsite
Cited with a line of al-Shanfarā using نِسْي for a dropped/left object.
On this basis Ibn Fāris reads نَسُوا اللَّهَ فَنَسِيَهُمْ (al-Tawba 67) and فَنَسِيَ (of Adam, Ṭāhā 115) as "leaving/abandoning"
highlights.note: the author's own exegesis of Q 9:67, 20:115

highlights.text: two root meanings: keeping close to something and mingling with it, and a rising in something
Al-qinw is the date-cluster (ʿidhq) with what is on it, so called because it keeps close to its tree.
Imruʾ al-Qays speaks of "the first (bikr) of al-muqānāt, whiteness mingled with yellow, nourished by wholesome water."
a single governing idea: **striking a thing**
A severe stroke of fortune, so named because it strikes people with its severity.
citing Aws: at every trench they leave an armoured man "dragged as the scab-ridden weanling is dragged."
a large, regular root whose core sense is returning / sending back (radd) and repetition (takrār)
رَجَعَ / يَرْجِعُ / رُجُوعًا (to go back, come back). الرُّجْعَى (al-rujʿā) is a noun meaning the returning.
the sky "returns" — it pours rain, then comes back and rains again
Illustrated by Ḥumayd's line imagining a dwelling that might "return an answer" to one who questions it.
assigns r-m-m four root meanings (uṣūl), arranged as two opposed pairs: gathering a thing together and mending it, against its wearing out; and silence, against its opposite
Al-ramīm is decayed bones, as in Q 36:78: "Who will give life to the bones when they are ramīm?"
In a verse of Aws, a man who marvels at the poet's people would, had war buffeted him, not have stirred his lips (lam yataramram).
saḥar (السَحَر) = the period just before dawn
a spell/enchantment (ukhdha). Al-Jawharī's defining principle: anything whose way of taking hold is subtle and fine is called siḥr.
Shāhid: Labīd's line calling mankind "sparrows of this musaḥḥar people."
al-Jawharī gives two readings — (a) musaḥḥar = one created with a lung (siḥr), i.e. a mortal like others; (b) one of the "beguiled / sustained with food."
the root meaning of s-b is cutting, and reviling was derived from it
a second root meaning length and extension
al-sabb is reviling, which he explains as a cutting: "there is no severance more severing than reviling"
cited from Abū Duʾād: "many a wide, empty wasteland (sabsab), over which its blowing dust runs"
citing al-Hudhalī: "he let himself down to it between a rope (sibb) and a cord"
around one core idea — soundness and well-being (ṣiḥḥa, ʿāfiya)
submission/compliance (inqiyād) — so called because the one who submits becomes free of refusal and resistance
Al-silm / al-salm (reconciliation, ṣulḥ)
Al-sullam (ladder): also traced to salāma, because someone climbing down is hoped to reach safety
Ibn Fāris reports that "the people of knowledge" call God al-Salām because He is free from the defect, deficiency, and perishing that affect created things.
one root whose single idea is **movement combined with shifting appearance or colour**
a bedouin youth present answered: "from their اخْتِيَال — their swaggering gait,"
"it looks as though it is such-and-such / it is made to appear to me (yukhayyalu ilayya) that it is so" — i.e. an impression, not a certainty
al-Shammākh: once you have carried me and my saddle to ʿArāba, choke on the blood of your own aorta.
zabad: foam/froth on a liquid, or (for milk) the cream/butter that rises and separates
each casts off its zabad/azbad ("foam(s)")
a saying calls it "more delicious than zabad with dates,"
Closing citation from Khudayr al-Hudhali: "the hida' (camel-driving song) is the zabad of the heart"
the Prophet is reported to have forbidden "the zabd of the polytheists" (accepting a gift/reward from them)
